subject: history_social
passage: In the early 1900s, the Harvard College Observatory hired women, known as "computers," to examine thousands of photographic plates of the night sky. The work was considered routine, and the pay was modest. Yet one of these women, Henrietta Swan Leavitt, noticed a pattern in a type of star whose brightness rises and falls: the longer such a star took to complete a cycle, the brighter it truly was. Her finding, published in 1912, later gave astronomers a way to measure distances to faraway stars and even to other galaxies.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Leavitt, hired for supposedly routine work, made a finding that helped astronomers measure great distances.
choices.B: Leavitt found that stars whose brightness rises and falls are farther away than other stars.
choices.C: Leavitt used her own finding to measure the distances to several galaxies beyond our own.
choices.D: The women hired as "computers" at Harvard were paid modest wages to examine photographs of the sky.

explanation.why: The text contrasts the job's low status ("considered routine," "modest" pay) with what Leavitt achieved through it, signaled by "Yet": she found a pattern that "later gave astronomers a way to measure distances." The main idea joins that contrast with the importance of her finding.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the contrast between the routine job and the far-reaching discovery Leavitt made.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Leavitt linked a star's cycle length to its true brightness; the text never says such stars are farther away.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says her finding "later gave astronomers" a method; it does not say she measured galaxies herself.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes the working conditions in the first two sentences but leaves out Leavitt's discovery.
